title: 03 · Test
text:
UNDERSTANDBUILDTESTDECIDEREFLECT





13:15 · Thandi Jacobs · Production Manager

I’m not convinced by Supplier C’s 78% self-consumption assumption.

Production varies during the week. If we cannot use as much solar power at the time it is generated as the supplier assumes, what happens to your recommendation?




Purpose → Outcome → Activity → Evidence



Purpose of this stage: move beyond a single spreadsheet answer by testing whether the decision is robust to uncertainty.


Outcome for this stage: Evaluate the sensitivity of an investment decision to a material operational assumption and interpret the implications for management.


You will demonstrate this by: distinguishing payback from NPV; changing System C’s self-consumption assumption; interpreting the resulting NPV changes; identifying the approximate crossover between Systems B and C; and identifying additional evidence required to validate the assumption.


Evidence: completed Test Assumptions!A7:E14, crossover interpretation and an evidence requirement concerning the factory load profile.





Excel + Google Sheets · Test


The SUMPRODUCT, ROW, MAX, MATCH and CHOOSE formulas below are written once and used unchanged in both applications.


<div class="platform"><strong>Excel</strong>Enter formulas in <span class="cell">B8:E8</span>; select the row and drag the fill handle down to row 14. Format <span class="cell">B8:D14</span> as rand currency.</div>
<div class="platform"><strong>Google Sheets</strong>Enter the same formulas in <span class="cell">B8:E8</span>; drag the fill handle down to row 14, or select <span class="cell">B8:E14</span> and use <strong>Fill down</strong> / <span class="kbd">Ctrl+D</span>. Format <span class="cell">B8:D14</span> via Format → Number → Currency.</div>


Do not “translate” the formulas. Sheet names, apostrophes, dollar signs and cell addresses remain exactly as printed.



Story so far: Your base model is complete. System A has the shortest payback. But management also wants to understand long-term value.



The case · Operations challenges the supplier assumption


“Will we really use 78% of System C’s output?”


Simple payback favours System A at about 2.92 years. A 20-year discounted cash-flow view tells a different story: under the base assumptions, System C has the highest NPV at about R2.871 million.


Why? Payback focuses on recovery speed. NPV considers the value today of future net savings over the full analysis period.


The Production Manager now questions System C’s 78% self-consumption. Your task is to stress-test that assumption.




Decision question

Does System C still create the most long-term value if Cape Manufacturing cannot use as much of its solar output as the supplier expects?



Excel instruction · sensitivity table


Work on the Test Assumptions sheet


The scenario rates are already entered in A8:A14: 78%, 75%, 72%, 70%, 68%, 65%, 60%.


Enter the following formulas in row 8. The formulas use SUMPRODUCT to value 20 years of escalating savings, degradation, maintenance and discounting. For this short course, you are using the discounted-cash-flow engine rather than being assessed on constructing it from first principles.


NPV A — Test Assumptions!B8


=SUMPRODUCT((‘Case Data’!$B\(15*(1-'Case Data'!\)B$7)(ROW($1:\(20)-1)*'Case Data'!\)B\(16*'Case Data'!\)B\(4*(1+'Case Data'!\)B$5)(ROW($1:\(20)-1)-'Case Data'!\)B\(17*(1+'Case Data'!\)B$8)(ROW($1:\(20)-1))/(1+'Case Data'!\)B$6)ROW($1:\(20))-'Case Data'!\)B$13


NPV B — Test Assumptions!C8


=SUMPRODUCT((‘Case Data’!$C\(15*(1-'Case Data'!\)B$7)(ROW($1:\(20)-1)*'Case Data'!\)C\(16*'Case Data'!\)B\(4*(1+'Case Data'!\)B$5)(ROW($1:\(20)-1)-'Case Data'!\)C\(17*(1+'Case Data'!\)B$8)(ROW($1:\(20)-1))/(1+'Case Data'!\)B$6)ROW($1:\(20))-'Case Data'!\)C$13


NPV C — Test Assumptions!D8


=SUMPRODUCT((‘Case Data’!$D\(15*(1-'Case Data'!\)B$7)^(ROW($1:\(20)-1)*\)A8*‘Case Data’!$B\(4*(1+'Case Data'!\)B$5)(ROW($1:\(20)-1)-'Case Data'!\)D\(17*(1+'Case Data'!\)B$8)(ROW($1:\(20)-1))/(1+'Case Data'!\)B$6)^ROW($1:\(20))-'Case Data'!\)D$13


Highest NPV — Test Assumptions!E8


=CHOOSE(MATCH(MAX(B8:D8),B8:D8,0),“System A”,“System B”,“System C”)



After entering the four formulas in B8:E8, select them.


Drag the fill handle down through row 14. Because System C’s formula uses $A8, the scenario row changes while column A stays fixed.


Format B8:D14 as rand currency with no decimals.

Formative checkpoint · find the crossover


Compare columns C and D in rows 8:14. The switch occurs between 75% and 72%.



Formative feedback · check your conclusion


System B overtakes System C at approximately 74% self-consumption. The modelled crossover is about 73.96%.





Interrogate the assumption, not just the number


Which would be more useful for validating self-consumption: annual electricity consumption, or half-hourly load data aligned with expected solar production?



Why half-hourly data?


Self-consumption depends on when electricity is used relative to solar generation. Annual totals can conceal a mismatch between midday PV production and the factory’s load profile.




Evidence produced: completed sensitivity table Test Assumptions!A7:E14 and a reasoned view on the operational data management still needs.


Next: turn conflicting evidence and uncertainty into an executive recommendation.

section: Commit to a prediction before you calculate
text:
Commit to a prediction before you calculate
Which measure would you inspect first if you had to advise the Financial Director before opening the spreadsheet?

Installed cost
System size
Gross generation
Annual saving
Payback

Write your choice in your workbook or notes. Do not revise it yet. You will return to this judgement after the sensitivity analysis.

There is no correct answer at this stage. The purpose is to make your initial reasoning visible before the model changes what you know.

title: 04 · Decide
text:
UNDERSTANDBUILDTESTDECIDEREFLECT




15:30 · Financial Director

I don’t need another spreadsheet. I need your recommendation.

Which system should we take forward, why, and what do we still need to verify? Keep it to 100 words.




Purpose → Outcome → Assessment criteria → Evidence



Purpose of this stage: integrate quantitative evidence, uncertainty and professional scepticism into a concise management recommendation.


Outcome for this stage: Formulate and communicate an evidence-based investment recommendation that integrates quantitative analysis, commercial trade-offs, uncertainty and professional scepticism.


Associated assessment criteria: a successful response identifies a proposal; uses at least two correctly interpreted quantitative results; explains one material trade-off; identifies an assumption requiring verification; distinguishes evidence from an unsupported supplier claim; and remains within 100 words.


Evidence: recommendation in Recommendation!A7 and professional-scepticism response in Recommendation!A22.





Excel + Google Sheets · Decide


<div class="platform"><strong>Excel</strong>Enter the recommendation in the response area beginning <span class="cell">Recommendation!A7</span>. Use Home → <strong>Wrap Text</strong> if necessary.</div>
<div class="platform"><strong>Google Sheets</strong>Enter the recommendation in the same response area beginning <span class="cell">Recommendation!A7</span>. Use Format → Wrapping → <strong>Wrap</strong> if necessary.</div>


Use the workbook cells as evidence rather than retyping numbers from memory. This audit trail is the same in both platforms.



Story so far: A is fastest on payback; C creates the greatest base-case NPV; B becomes preferable to C if C’s self-consumption falls below roughly 74%.



The case · The Financial Director wants a recommendation


The spreadsheet gives evidence. It does not choose the decision rule.


You now have a genuine commercial trade-off. Management needs a recommendation that distinguishes measured results from assumptions still requiring verification.

Excel instruction · use the workbook as evidence


Do not retype numbers from memory



Payback evidence: Your Model!B7:D7.


Base NPV evidence: first scenario row Test Assumptions!B8:D8.


Sensitivity evidence: Test Assumptions!A8:E14.


Write your final recommendation in the merged response area beginning at Recommendation!A7 (displayed across A7:F13).



Use Wrap Text if needed. Keep the recommendation to 100 words or fewer.




Executive briefing task · ≤100 words

Recommend one proposal to the Financial Director.



Name the selected proposal.


Use at least two quantified pieces of Excel evidence.


State one explicit commercial trade-off.


Name one unverified operational assumption that must be confirmed before contract signature.



There is no single acceptable recommendation if the reasoning is coherent, quantified and appropriately qualified.



Professional scepticism · Supplier C’s environmental claim


Supplier C states that its panels have a lower lifecycle environmental impact but provides no independently verified evidence.


What evidence would you request before allowing the claim to influence the recommendation?




Excel instruction · record your scepticism response


Go to Recommendation!A22 (merged across A22:F26) and type your response. Consider lifecycle methodology, manufacturing impacts, expected service life, recyclability, independent certification, system boundaries and the basis of comparison with A and B.



Evidence produced: ≤100-word recommendation in Recommendation!A7 + evidence request in Recommendation!A22.



Pre-submission check


Before you send the briefing

 I selected one proposal.  I used at least two quantified spreadsheet results.  I stated one material commercial trade-off.  I identified one unverified operational assumption.  I treated Supplier C’s environmental claim as a claim requiring evidence.  My recommendation is 100 words or fewer.


Next: audit your outputs, explain the trade-off and transfer the modelling pattern.

title: 02 · Build
text:
UNDERSTANDBUILDTESTDECIDEREFLECT





09:40 · Financial Director

Before we discuss NPV, give me a clean Year-1 comparison.

I want to see what each system produces economically, what it saves after maintenance, and how quickly the capital is recovered. Keep the model traceable to the source data.




Purpose → Outcome → Activity → Evidence



Purpose of this stage: convert supplier and case data into comparable financial measures using an auditable spreadsheet structure.


Outcome for this stage: Construct an auditable spreadsheet model that converts operational solar data into comparable Year-1 financial measures.


You will demonstrate this by: calculating useful generation, gross and net Year-1 savings and simple payback; applying relative and absolute references appropriately; formatting outputs consistently; and creating a decision-relevant visual.


Evidence: completed Your Model!B4:D8, one comparison chart and a one-sentence visual-design rationale.





Excel + Google Sheets · Build


All formulas on this page are identical. Enter them in the same cells and copy them across in the same direction.


<div class="platform"><strong>Excel formatting</strong>Select <span class="cell">B5:D6</span> → Home → Number and choose Currency/Accounting. Select <span class="cell">B7:D7</span> and show two decimal places.</div>
<div class="platform"><strong>Google Sheets formatting</strong>Select <span class="cell">B5:D6</span> → Format → Number → Currency (or use the currency toolbar button). Select <span class="cell">B7:D7</span> → Format → Number → Number and set two decimal places.</div>



Story so far: You understand the inputs and have entered your first formula. Now complete the chain from operating data to payback.



The case · The Financial Director wants comparable numbers


Turn three supplier proposals into one auditable model


Management needs a common basis for comparison. Build the logic in the Your Model sheet: useful generation → gross saving → net saving → simple payback.





1



Useful generation — already started


Useful generation = Year-1 generation × self-consumption


Cells: Your Model!B4:D4


System A formula in B4:


=‘Case Data’!B15*‘Case Data’!B16


Copy B4 across to D4. Relative references should change automatically.







2



Gross Year-1 saving


Gross saving = useful generation × tariff


Select Your Model!B5 and enter:


=B4*‘Case Data’!$B\(4</div>
<p>Copy across to <span class="cell">D5</span>. The first reference changes B4 → C4 → D4; the tariff stays locked at <span class="cell">Case Data!\)B$4.



Formative feedback · check values


B5 = R231,840; C5 = R287,980; D5 = R321,048.








3



Net Year-1 saving


Net saving = gross saving − maintenance


In Your Model!B6 enter:


=B5-‘Case Data’!B17


Copy across to D6. Format B6:D6 as rand currency.



Formative feedback · check values


B6 = R222,840; C6 = R276,980; D6 = R307,048.








4



Simple payback


Simple payback = installed cost ÷ Net Year-1 saving


In Your Model!B7 enter:


=‘Case Data’!B13/B6


Copy across to D7. Format B7:D7 to two decimal places.



Formative feedback · diagnose your result


Your answers should be approximately A = 2.92, B = 2.96, C = 3.22 years. If not, check percentage formats, cell references, subtraction of maintenance, and numerator/denominator.







Optional Excel skill · rank the paybacks


Use a function rather than ranking by eye


In Your Model!B8 enter:


=RANK.EQ(B7,$B\(7:\)D$7,1)


Copy across to D8. The final argument 1 means the smallest payback receives rank 1.



Formative feedback · check ranks


System A = 1, System B = 2, System C = 3.





Visual communication task


Create one chart an executive can read in five seconds



Decide which single comparison your chart should communicate.


For a simple-payback chart, use proposal names B3:D3 and payback values B7:D7.




ExcelSelect B3:D3, then add the non-adjacent B7:D7 range using Ctrl (Windows) or ⌘ (Mac). Choose Insert → Column or Bar Chart → Clustered Column.


Google SheetsThe simplest beginner route is to create a small temporary two-row chart source in unused cells (for example H3:J4): copy the three proposal names into row 3 and link row 4 to B7:D7. Select H3:J4 → Insert → Chart → choose Column chart in the Chart editor. This avoids awkward non-adjacent selection.




Give the chart a decision-focused title such as Simple payback by proposal.


Remove anything that does not help a manager compare the three systems.



Write one sentence: “I chose to show ___ because ___.”



Evidence produced: completed Your Model!B4:D8 + one chart + one-sentence design rationale.


Next: management challenges an assumption. Test whether your conclusion survives.

title: Spreadsheet Essentials
text:
UNDERSTANDBUILDTESTDECIDEREFLECT





Enabling outcomes · spreadsheet readiness



Purpose of this section: provide the minimum spreadsheet skills needed to complete the investment analysis. No prior Excel or Google Sheets proficiency is assumed.


After completing this section, you should be able to:



identify a cell using its column and row address;


enter and edit a formula;


reference data on another worksheet;


distinguish and apply relative, absolute and mixed references;


copy formulas accurately;


apply appropriate number formats; and


inspect a formula to identify a possible error.



Evidence: a correct first useful-generation calculation in Your Model!B4:D4 and successful readiness check.





Platform guide · keep this beside you


<div class="platform"><strong>Microsoft Excel</strong>
  <ul><li>Start a formula: type <span class="cell">=</span>.</li>
  <li>Edit a cell: double-click it or use the Formula Bar.</li>
  <li>Copy a formula: drag the fill handle; <span class="kbd">Ctrl+D</span> fills down on Windows.</li>
  <li>Cycle relative/absolute references while editing: <span class="kbd">F4</span>; on Mac, <span class="kbd">F4</span> or <span class="kbd">⌘T</span> depending on keyboard settings.</li>
  <li>Undo: <span class="kbd">Ctrl+Z</span> / <span class="kbd">⌘Z</span>.</li></ul>
</div>
<div class="platform"><strong>Google Sheets</strong>
  <ul><li>Start a formula: type <span class="cell">=</span>.</li>
  <li>Edit a cell: double-click it or use the formula bar.</li>
  <li>Copy a formula: drag the fill handle; <span class="kbd">Ctrl+D</span> fills down and <span class="kbd">Ctrl+R</span> fills right on Windows/ChromeOS.</li>
  <li>Cycle relative/absolute references while editing: <span class="kbd">F4</span>; on many Macs use <span class="kbd">Fn+F4</span>.</li>
  <li>Undo: <span class="kbd">Ctrl+Z</span> / <span class="kbd">⌘Z</span>. Changes are saved automatically.</li></ul>
</div>


Same conceptual rule: B15 is relative, $B\(4</span> is absolute, and <span class="cell">\)A8 fixes only the column. Dollar signs have the same meaning in both applications.



Story so far: You know what the proposal data mean. Now learn the spreadsheet mechanics needed to turn those inputs into a model.



Excel bridge · just enough Excel to start modelling


You do not need to know Excel or Google Sheets before continuing


You need five moves: select a cell, enter a formula, reference another sheet, copy a formula across, and format a result. You will practise each move on the actual Cape Manufacturing workbook.





1 · Cells and addresses


Columns use letters; rows use numbers. Their intersection is a cell. B4 means column B, row 4.


Click Case Data!B4. The Name Box identifies the active cell.




2 · Formulas begin with =


Excel calculates only when an entry begins with =.


Example: =2+3 returns 5. In this course, however, you will reference cells rather than type business inputs into formulas.




3 · Referencing another sheet


A reference such as ‘Case Data’!B15 means “use the value in cell B15 on the Case Data sheet”.


The quotation marks appear because the sheet name contains a space.




4 · Relative vs absolute


B15 is relative: copied one column right, it becomes C15.


$B$4 is absolute: copied anywhere, it remains B4. Use this for the shared tariff.





Guided practice · your first live formula


Calculate System A useful generation



Click the Your Model sheet.


Select the yellow cell B4.


Type exactly:



=‘Case Data’!B15*‘Case Data’!B16



Press Enter. You should see 82,800.


Click B4 again. Move the pointer to the small square at the bottom-right corner of the selection (the fill handle). Both Excel and Google Sheets use this control.


Drag the fill handle across to D4. In Google Sheets you can alternatively select B4:D4 and use Fill right / Ctrl+R where supported. Excel should adapt the relative references for Systems B and C.




Check the three values


B4 = 82,800, C4 = 102,850, D4 = 114,660.





Formatting essentials


Values and presentation are different things



Use Currency/Accounting formatting for rand amounts.


Use Percentage formatting for rates such as 90%.


Use Number with two decimal places for payback years.


Do not type “R”, “%” or “years” into numeric cells; use number formats so Excel can still calculate with the values.




If you make a mistake: use Undo (Ctrl+Z on Windows; ⌘Z on Mac). A formula can always be edited in the cell or Formula Bar.


Formative readiness check: you can now enter a formula, read a cross-sheet reference, copy a relative formula and recognise an absolute reference.


Next: use those moves to complete the commercial model.

title: Reviewer Rationale
text:
UNDERSTANDBUILDTESTDECIDEREFLECT




South African OBE design statement



Constructive alignment is made visible


The activity is organised around explicit intended learning outcomes, authentic learning activities, formative checkpoints, associated assessment criteria and observable evidence of achievement. The narrative is the professional context through which the outcomes are developed; it does not replace the curriculum structure.


The design deliberately integrates foundational competence (understanding concepts and assumptions), practical competence (performing spreadsheet and analytical tasks) and reflexive competence (adapting reasoning, evaluating uncertainty and transferring learning).


The activity is best described as designed in accordance with South African outcomes-based and constructive-alignment principles. It should not be represented as independently “CHE accredited” or as an NQF-registered qualification. Exact formal module-level alignment would require the approved Stellenbosch module outcomes, assessment plan and institutional curriculum documentation.





Reviewer note


One case, one evolving model, one professional decision


The activity is structured as a continuous workplace narrative. The learner receives imperfect supplier information, constructs a transparent spreadsheet model, encounters a challenge to an assumption, stress-tests the model, communicates a recommendation and reflects on transfer.


The five-step arc is Understand → Build → Test → Decide → Reflect. The separate Spreadsheet Essentials bridge supports true beginners in either Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets without turning the activity into a generic software tutorial.

SAICA competency alignment


This activity is designed to evidence publicly documented SAICA competencies associated with the former CA2025 framework, now described by SAICA as the CA of the Future Competency Framework. It particularly integrates:




Digital acumen


Digital user skills: using technology as an enabler of decision-making; data analysis and spreadsheet modelling; deliberate use of formulas, references and visual communication.




Decision-making acumen


Analytical and critical thinking, weighing alternatives, integrated thinking, numerical reasoning and judgement.




Professional scepticism


Questioning supplier assumptions and unsupported claims, identifying evidence gaps and withholding reliance until appropriate evidence is obtained.





Why this is Digital- and Leadership Acumen


Digital acumen is treated as more than software proficiency. The learner uses a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets) to structure information, make logic auditable, interrogate uncertainty and communicate evidence. Leadership/professional acumen enters when the learner must make a qualified recommendation despite competing criteria and incomplete evidence.



Associated assessment criteria & formative feedback




Criterion

Scepticism/reflection

Alignment note: this is a non-credit application demonstration. The public sources support alignment with Stellenbosch’s Digital- and Leadership Acumen context and SAICA’s competency language, but exact module-level constructive alignment would require the formally approved module outcomes and assessment plan.


Publicly documented curriculum context



Stellenbosch School of Accountancy includes Digital- and Leadership Acumen modules in its accountancy programmes, including modules focused on data analytics for accountants.


SAICA defines digital user skills as using technology ethically to optimise decision-making and business efficiencies, and defines decision-making competencies including analytical thinking, critical thinking, integrated thinking and judgement.


SAICA describes professional scepticism as questioning information, remaining alert to possible error or fraud, and critically evaluating evidence.



Sources for reviewer verification: SAICA CA of the Future / Competencies Defined; SAICA IAC competency framework; Stellenbosch School of Accountancy programme information.



Platform design rationale


Spreadsheet reasoning is the competence; software menus are scaffolding


The activity deliberately preserves identical formulas, sheet names and cell addresses across Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Platform-specific guidance is limited to interface operations such as opening/saving, number formatting, filling formulas and chart creation.


This allows the learner to demonstrate transferable digital acumen rather than success being contingent on prior familiarity with one vendor interface.




V7 interaction design


Interactivity is tied to evidence of learning


The interactive elements are deliberately sparse and purposeful: a pre-model prediction activates prior conceptions; formula reveals support guided practice; management messages maintain authentic workplace narrative; sensitivity interpretation requires judgement rather than calculation alone; the pre-submission checklist makes assessment criteria visible; and the final reflection closes the prediction-feedback-transfer loop.


Decorative interaction has been avoided. Each interaction either elicits evidence, provides formative feedback, scaffolds performance or strengthens transfer.



Design principle: technical spreadsheet skills are introduced at the point where the case creates a reason to use them.
